questions.question: Which property is NOT due to hydrogen bonding? A: ice is less dense than water at 0 deg C; B: HF has a higher boiling temperature than HCl; C: H-H bond enthalpy is greater than Si-H bond enthalpy; D: alcohols are less volatile than alkanes of similar molar mass.
questions.answer: C (H-H bond enthalpy is greater than Si-H bond enthalpy)

B: HF molecules hydrogen bond to each other, so HF boils higher than HCl - due to hydrogen bonding.
D: alcohols hydrogen bond between molecules, so they are less volatile than alkanes - due to hydrogen bonding.
C: bond enthalpy is the energy of a covalent bond within a molecule, not an intermolecular force.
So the answer is C.

questions.answer: More carbon atoms give more electrons and a larger molecule, so London forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
steps: Alkane molecules are non-polar, so the only intermolecular forces between them are London forces.
Larger alkanes have more electrons, so their electron clouds are more polarisable.
More polarisable molecules form larger instantaneous and induced dipoles, so London forces are stronger.
Longer chains have a larger surface area of contact between neighbouring molecules, giving more London force interactions.
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger London forces and separate the molecules.
So boiling temperature increases with the number of carbon atoms.

questions.question: 1 kg of petrol is assumed to be pure octane, with standard enthalpy change of combustion -5470 kJ mol-1. The energy used to move the car is 11 MJ. Calculate the percentage of the maximum energy that is available to move the car.
steps: Molar mass of octane, C8H18 = (8 x 12.0) + (18 x 1.0) = 114 g mol-1.
Moles of octane in 1000 g = 1000 / 114 = 8.77 mol.
Maximum energy from 1 kg = 8.77 x 5470 kJ = approx. 48 000 kJ = 48.0 MJ.
Percentage available = (11 / 48.0) x 100 = 22.9%, which is about 23%.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the intermolecular forces involved when hydrogen and ammonia liquefy, describing how these forces are formed.
questions.answer: Hydrogen has only London forces from temporary dipoles; ammonia has hydrogen bonds (N-H...N) and dipole-dipole forces as well as London forces, so ammonia liquefies more easily.
steps: Hydrogen is a non-polar molecule, so its only intermolecular forces are London forces.
London forces form when electron movement creates a temporary dipole that induces dipoles in neighbouring molecules.
These forces are weak because H2 has only two electrons, so hydrogen must be cooled to very low temperatures to liquefy.
Ammonia is polar (N-H bonds and a lone pair on N), so it has permanent dipole-dipole forces between molecules.
Ammonia also forms hydrogen bonds: the lone pair on N attracts the delta+ H of a neighbouring N-H group.
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than London forces, so ammonia liquefies more easily than hydrogen.
Contrast: both are intermolecular, but H2 has only London forces while NH3 also has hydrogen bonds and dipole-dipole forces.
